entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To start to fail or fall apart, often gradually, as one problem leads to another.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and storytelling about plans, deals, marriages and careers: *the deal began to unravel*, *his life unraveled*. In this sense it has no object and often follows *begin to* or *start to*. American spelling has one *l*: *unraveled*, *unraveling*.
entries.pattern: something begins / starts to unravel; unravel quickly / completely
examples: Their marriage began to **unravel** after he took a job in another state.
The team's season **unraveled** after their quarterback got hurt in October.
The company's story started to **unravel** when journalists checked its sales figures.

drill.sentence: Our vacation plans started to {{unravel}} when the airline canceled our flight and the hotel lost our reservation.
drill.hint: fail bit by bit, one problem after another (not *collapse* or *crumble*)

entries.related: *fall apart* — the informal equivalent; *disintegrate* — break into pieces, stronger; *unravel a mystery* — a different sense, solve it.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: So strong or obvious that it seems you could almost touch it; easy for everyone to notice.
entries.usage: Very common in journalism and descriptive writing about the mood in a room or crowd: *palpable tension*, *palpable excitement*, *palpable relief*. Writers use it to show that everyone could sense the emotion without anyone saying it. In medicine it has a literal sense, able to be felt by touch (*a palpable lump*).
entries.pattern: palpable tension / excitement / relief / fear; a palpable sense of something
examples: When my ex walked into the party, the awkwardness was **palpable**.
There was a **palpable** sense of relief when the missing hikers were found alive.
As the final seconds ticked away, a **palpable** buzz spread through the stadium.

drill.sentence: When the judge walked in to read the verdict, the tension in the courtroom was {{palpable}}.
drill.hint: so strong you could almost touch it (not *thick* or *high*)

entries.related: *tangible* — real and concrete, often about results or benefits; *obvious* — plainer; *imperceptible* — the opposite, too small to notice.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Involved with others in a wrongful act, for example by helping, allowing or staying silent about it.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, ethics and serious discussion: *complicit in the cover-up*, *complicit in fraud*. It is often used to criticize people who did not commit the act themselves but knew and did nothing (*silence makes us complicit*). It usually takes *in*, and the noun is *complicity*.
entries.pattern: be complicit in something; complicit silence
examples: By staying quiet about the cheating, the other players became **complicit** in it.
The bank was accused of being **complicit** in money laundering for years.
I felt **complicit** for laughing at the joke, even though I didn't tell it.

drill.sentence: The other parents knew their kids were bullying him and did nothing, which made them {{complicit}} in it.
drill.hint: sharing the guilt for a wrong (not *involved* or *accomplices*)

entries.related: *accomplice* — a person who helps commit a crime; *implicated* — shown to be involved; *innocent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Making someone or something very weak and unable to function normally.
entries.usage: Common in medical, news and personal writing about illness, pain and fear: *debilitating migraines*, *a debilitating illness*, *debilitating anxiety*. It is stronger than *serious*: it means the condition stops you from living normally. It is also used for problems that weaken organizations (*a debilitating shortage of staff*).
entries.pattern: a debilitating illness / condition / injury; debilitating pain / migraines / anxiety
examples: She gets **debilitating** migraines that keep her in a dark room for two days.
For some people, stage fright is so **debilitating** that they turn down promotions.
A **debilitating** shortage of nurses has forced the hospital to close one of its wards.

drill.sentence: His back pain was so {{debilitating}} that he couldn't tie his own shoes for a month.
drill.hint: making him too weak to function (not *severe*, *crippling* or *disabling*)

entries.related: *crippling* — very close, often about costs or fear; *disabling* — causing long-term disability; *invigorating* — the opposite, giving energy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Opposite to what is reasonable, expected or intended, often in a way that seems strange or even deliberate.
entries.usage: Common in economics, policy writing and journalism: *perverse incentives*, *a perverse effect*, *perverse logic*. People also *take a perverse pleasure in* something that others would hate. Unlike German *pervers*, it rarely has a sexual meaning; that sense belongs to *perverted*.
entries.pattern: a perverse incentive / effect / result; take a perverse pleasure in something
examples: Paying hospitals per test creates a **perverse** incentive to order tests that patients don't need.
I take a **perverse** pleasure in cleaning out the garage on a rainy Sunday.
In a **perverse** twist, the new highway made traffic worse by attracting more drivers.

drill.sentence: The daycare's new late-pickup fee had the {{perverse}} effect of making parents arrive late more often.
drill.hint: contrary to what was intended (not *unintended*, *ironic* or *paradoxical*)

entries.related: *counterproductive* — having the opposite of the desired effect; *contrary* — deliberately doing the opposite; *perverted* — sexually abnormal, a different word.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Describing an imagined future society, or a real situation, that is frightening, unjust or oppressive.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, journalism and everyday talk: *a dystopian novel*, *a dystopian future*, *it feels a bit dystopian*. People now use it loosely for real things that feel cold, controlled or nightmarish, such as heavy surveillance or an orange, smoke-filled sky. The opposite is *utopian*, and the noun is *dystopia*.
entries.pattern: a dystopian novel / film / future / world; feel / look dystopian
examples: My son is reading a **dystopian** novel about a future where teenagers are forced to fight each other on live TV.
With smoke from the wildfires turning the sky orange, the city looked downright **dystopian**.
Some people find it a little **dystopian** that their fridge can now track what they eat.

drill.sentence: The movie imagines a {{dystopian}} world where people have to pay for every breath of clean air.
drill.hint: frightening and oppressive, the reverse of an ideal society (not *bleak* or *nightmarish*)

entries.related: *utopian* — about an ideal society, often unrealistic; *Orwellian* — about state control and propaganda; *apocalyptic* — about the end of the world.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make a process, system or organization simpler and more efficient, usually by removing unnecessary steps.
entries.usage: Very common in business, government and tech language: *streamline the process*, *streamline operations*, *a streamlined application*. It sounds positive but is sometimes a polite word for job cuts. It is also used for physical shape: a *streamlined* car moves easily through the air.
entries.pattern: streamline a process / procedure / operations; a streamlined version
examples: The DMV has **streamlined** license renewals, so you can now do the whole thing online.
We **streamlined** our morning routine by laying out the kids' clothes the night before.
The new CEO wants to **streamline** the company, which everyone knows means layoffs.

drill.sentence: The hospital {{streamlined}} its check-in process, and the wait in the ER dropped from two hours to forty minutes.
drill.hint: made simpler and more efficient (not *simplified*)

entries.related: *simplify* — more general; *optimize* — make as effective as possible, more technical; *overcomplicate* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Needing a lot of effort and energy over a long time; hard and tiring.
entries.usage: Used in writing and educated speech about journeys, climbs, processes and tasks: *an arduous journey*, *an arduous process*, *arduous training*. It suggests long, physically or mentally exhausting effort rather than intellectual difficulty. In conversation, people more often say *grueling* or *exhausting*.
entries.pattern: an arduous journey / climb / process / task
examples: After an **arduous** six-hour climb, we reached the summit just as the clouds rolled in.
Adopting a child from abroad can be an **arduous** process that takes years.
The study required an **arduous** manual review of thousands of medical records.

drill.sentence: Renovating the old farmhouse ourselves was an {{arduous}} project that took three summers.
drill.hint: long, hard and tiring (not *exhausting* or *enormous*)

entries.related: *grueling* — very tiring, often about schedules or races; *strenuous* — needing physical effort; *effortless* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short period of rest or relief from something difficult or unpleasant.
entries.usage: Common in news, weather reports and caregiving language: *a brief respite from the heat*, *a welcome respite*, and *respite care* for families who look after sick or disabled relatives. It usually takes *from* and suggests that the difficulty will return. Most Americans say RES-pit; rih-SPYTE is also heard.
entries.pattern: a (brief / welcome) respite from something; respite care
examples: The afternoon thunderstorm brought a brief **respite** from the heat.
**Respite** care gives parents of disabled children a few hours of rest each week.
For the nurses, the quiet night shift was a welcome **respite** after a chaotic week.

drill.sentence: The kids' week at summer camp gave us a welcome {{respite}} from constant fights over screen time.
drill.hint: short pause from something hard (not *break*, *rest*, *relief* or *reprieve*)

entries.related: *reprieve* — a delay or cancellation of something bad, like a punishment; *lull* — a quiet period in activity; *break* — the everyday word.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Freedom from punishment or bad consequences for doing something wrong.
entries.usage: Almost always in the phrase *with impunity*, common in news, law and human-rights reporting: *act with impunity*, *break the rules with impunity*. It suggests that the people responsible know they will not be caught or punished. *A culture of impunity* is a frequent phrase in serious journalism.
entries.pattern: with impunity; act / operate / break the law with impunity; a culture of impunity
examples: Drivers on our street speed with **impunity** because there's never a police car around.
For years, the gang operated with **impunity** because local officials were taking bribes.
My little brother could break anything in the house with **impunity**; I always got the blame.

drill.sentence: Our cat walks across the kitchen counter with {{impunity}}, because he knows nobody will do anything about it.
drill.hint: no fear of being punished (not *ease*)

entries.related: *immunity* — legal protection from prosecution; *with abandon* — without control or care; *accountability* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To improve and refine a skill over time through practice.
entries.usage: Common in career, sports and arts writing: *hone your skills*, *hone your craft*, *a finely honed sense of humor*. It suggests long, careful practice that makes a good skill sharper, as a knife is sharpened. The participle is common before nouns (*well-honed instincts*).
entries.pattern: hone + skills / craft / technique / instincts; finely / well honed
examples: She spent years **honing** her craft in small comedy clubs before getting her own show.
He **honed** his cooking skills by making dinner for his roommates every night.
Few people have such a finely **honed** sense of what customers want.

drill.sentence: The violinist practices six hours a day to {{hone}} her technique before the big competition.
drill.hint: make even better through long practice (not *sharpen*, *perfect*, *polish* or *refine*)

entries.related: *sharpen* — very close, more common in speech; *refine* — make small improvements. *Hone in on* (focus on) is common in American speech, but many editors prefer *home in on*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To accept or allow behavior that is morally wrong or offensive, as if it were acceptable.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, journalism and official statements, and very often negative: *we do not condone violence*, *I don't condone what he did, but…*. It means tolerating or excusing something wrong, not actively supporting it. It is not used for approving good things.
entries.pattern: not condone + violence / cheating / behavior; I don't condone X, but …
examples: I don't **condone** what he did, but I understand why he was so angry.
The team issued a statement saying it does not **condone** the players' behavior at the nightclub.
By laughing along with his cruel jokes, the other guests were basically **condoning** them.

drill.sentence: Her parents don't {{condone}} lying, but they ignore small white lies told to spare someone's feelings.
drill.hint: treat a wrong as acceptable (not *tolerate* or *allow*)

mistake.wrong: The principal condoned the vandalism in the strongest terms.
mistake.right: The principal condemned the vandalism in the strongest terms.
mistake.why: The two words look alike but are nearly opposite: *condemn* means criticize strongly, *condone* means accept or excuse.

entries.related: *tolerate* — put up with, not necessarily something wrong; *turn a blind eye to* — pretend not to see; *condemn* — the opposite, criticize strongly.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To turn criticism, attention, blame or a question away from yourself, often to avoid dealing with it.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports interviews and talk about relationships: *deflect criticism*, *deflect blame*, *deflect attention from*, *deflect a question*. It usually suggests evasion; in casual speech people say *you're deflecting* when someone changes the subject. Literally, it means to make a moving object change direction (*the goalie deflected the shot*).
entries.pattern: deflect + criticism / blame / attention / questions (away from oneself / onto someone)
examples: Every time I ask about his ex, he makes a joke to **deflect** the question.
The coach tried to **deflect** blame for the loss onto the referees.
The company's statement seemed designed to **deflect** attention from the data breach.

drill.sentence: When I asked my teenager about the dent in the car, she {{deflected}} by asking why I never let her drive.
drill.hint: turned attention away from herself (not *countered* or *dodged*)

entries.related: *dodge* — avoid a question, informal; *evade* — avoid answering or dealing with, more formal; *take responsibility* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very basic and not fully developed; only the simplest level of knowledge, skill or equipment.
entries.usage: Common in writing and educated speech about knowledge and tools: *a rudimentary knowledge of Spanish*, *rudimentary tools*, *rudimentary medical care*. It is a modest way to describe a low level, often used about yourself (*my German is rudimentary*). It sounds more formal than *basic*.
entries.pattern: a rudimentary knowledge / understanding of something; rudimentary tools / equipment / care
examples: I have only a **rudimentary** knowledge of Italian, enough to order coffee and ask for directions.
The cabin had **rudimentary** facilities: a wood stove, a sink and an outhouse.
The first version of the app was pretty **rudimentary**, but people loved it anyway.

drill.sentence: The village clinic could offer only {{rudimentary}} care, so serious cases were flown to the city.
drill.hint: of the simplest, most undeveloped kind (not *basic*, *limited* or *minimal*)

entries.related: *basic* — the everyday word; *elementary* — simple, often about school-level knowledge; *primitive* — very simple and early, can sound negative; *sophisticated* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Showing a careless lack of concern about something important, such as other people's safety, feelings or rights.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and serious conversation, and always critical: *a cavalier attitude toward safety*, *cavalier about money*, *cavalier treatment of the facts*. It suggests arrogance as well as carelessness. Typical patterns are *a cavalier attitude toward* something and *be cavalier about* something.
entries.pattern: a cavalier attitude toward / to something; be cavalier about something
examples: His **cavalier** attitude toward deadlines drives the rest of the team crazy.
She was surprisingly **cavalier** about leaving her front door unlocked in a big city.
Critics accused the company of a **cavalier** approach to customer privacy.

drill.sentence: My brother is so {{cavalier}} about money that he once lent his entire paycheck to a guy he'd met that week.
drill.hint: carelessly unconcerned, almost arrogant (not *careless* or *casual*)

entries.related: *casual* — relaxed, not always critical; *offhand* — careless in manner, about remarks; *reckless* — taking dangerous risks; *conscientious* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Understood or enjoyed by only a small group of people with special knowledge or interests.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, often slightly apologetic or critical: *an esoteric topic*, *esoteric jokes*, *a somewhat esoteric point*. Its everyday meaning is *obscure and specialized*. For German *Esoterik* (crystals, energy healing), English usually says *New Age*.
entries.pattern: an esoteric topic / subject / hobby / interest; esoteric to outsiders
examples: His podcast covers **esoteric** topics like the history of the paperclip and medieval tax law.
Wine labels can be **esoteric**, full of terms that only sommeliers seem to understand.
To most people, arguments about tabs versus spaces in code seem incredibly **esoteric**.

drill.sentence: My uncle collects old train timetables, which is about as {{esoteric}} as a hobby can get.
drill.hint: known or loved by only a tiny group (not *obscure*, *niche* or *eccentric*)

entries.related: *obscure* — little known, more general; *arcane* — known by few and hard to understand, often old; *niche* — appealing to a small, specialized market.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Strong dislike or hostility between people or groups, often lasting a long time.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and conversation about rivalries, families and workplaces: *animosity between*, *animosity toward*, *personal animosity*. It describes active ill feeling, stronger than *dislike*. It is often used in negatives to calm things down: *There's no animosity between us*.
entries.pattern: animosity between A and B; animosity toward someone; no animosity
examples: The **animosity** between the two coaches goes back to a fight in college.
There's no **animosity** between me and my ex; we just grew apart.
The decision to close the plant created lasting **animosity** toward the company in town.

drill.sentence: Years after the lawsuit, there was still deep {{animosity}} between the two neighbors over the fence.
drill.hint: mutual ill will (not *hostility*, *resentment* or *bitterness*)

entries.related: *hostility* — very close, can also mean aggressive acts; *resentment* — bitterness about unfair treatment, often one-sided; *goodwill* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well and communicate easily.
entries.usage: Common in workplace, teaching, healthcare and sales language: *build rapport*, *a good rapport with*, *an instant rapport*. It usually takes *with* (*rapport with patients*) or *between*. The final *t* is silent, as in French.
entries.pattern: build / establish rapport (with someone); a good / instant rapport (between people)
examples: The best nurses build **rapport** with patients quickly, even during a short visit.
My daughter and her new piano teacher had an instant **rapport**.
The two lead actors have such an easy **rapport** that the whole movie feels effortless.

drill.sentence: Our new neighbor has a great {{rapport}} with the kids on the block; they all run to her porch after school.
drill.hint: mutual understanding and easy friendship (not *bond*, *connection*, *way* or *relationship*)

mistake.wrong: I'll send you the rapport on the site visit by Friday.
mistake.right: I'll send you the report on the site visit by Friday.
mistake.why: In English, *rapport* only means a good relationship; a written account is a *report*, although French *rapport* and German *Rapport* can mean a report.

entries.related: *chemistry* — informal, natural attraction or understanding; *bond* — a close, lasting connection; *friction* — the opposite, tension between people.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a very forceful, passionate and emotional way, especially when disagreeing or denying something.
entries.usage: Common in news reports, especially with verbs of disagreement: *vehemently deny*, *vehemently oppose*, *vehemently disagree*, *vehemently object*. It is stronger than *strongly* and suggests visible emotion. The *h* is silent: VEE-uh-munt-lee.
entries.pattern: vehemently deny / oppose / disagree / object (to)
examples: The actor **vehemently** denied the rumors and threatened to sue the magazine.
Residents **vehemently** opposed the plan to build a parking garage next to the park.
My sister and I **vehemently** disagree about whether pineapple belongs on pizza.

drill.sentence: The restaurant {{vehemently}} denies that it reuses bread from customers' tables.
drill.hint: with fierce, passionate force (not *strongly*, *flatly* or *adamantly*)

entries.related: *strongly* — the neutral equivalent; *adamantly* — firmly, without changing your mind; *fiercely* — with intense energy, also used for loyalty and competition.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Large, heavy or complicated, and therefore slow, awkward or inefficient to use or do.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and business writing about objects, processes and systems: *a cumbersome process*, *cumbersome bureaucracy*, *cumbersome equipment*. It suggests that something wastes time or energy because of its size or complexity. It describes things and procedures, not people; a person who moves awkwardly is *clumsy*.
entries.pattern: a cumbersome process / procedure / system; cumbersome equipment
examples: Applying for a building permit in our town is a **cumbersome** process with six different forms.
Our old car seat was so **cumbersome** that moving it between cars took twenty minutes.
The old reporting tool was so **cumbersome** that analysts exported everything to Excel instead.

drill.sentence: Our old tent was too {{cumbersome}} to carry on long hikes, so we finally bought a light one.
drill.hint: big and hard to handle (not *bulky*, *heavy*, *awkward* or *unwieldy*)

entries.related: *unwieldy* — hard to handle because of size or shape; *bulky* — large and taking up space; *streamlined* — the opposite for processes.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way, often a way that is not ideal.
entries.usage: Common in academic, legal and journalistic writing, and used humorously in conversation: *a propensity for violence*, *a propensity to exaggerate*. It takes *for* + noun or *-ing*, or *to* + verb. Because it often describes bad habits, it can sound critical.
entries.pattern: a propensity for something / for -ing; a propensity to + verb
examples: My grandfather has a **propensity** to tell the same story at every family dinner.
The bike's main flaw is its **propensity** for flat tires on gravel roads.
Economists study the **propensity** to save, which tends to rise with income.

drill.sentence: Our dog has an unfortunate {{propensity}} for rolling in anything that smells bad.
drill.hint: built-in inclination (not *tendency*, *penchant* or *fondness*)

entries.related: *tendency* — the everyday word; *penchant* — a strong liking, usually harmless; *proclivity* — very close, often about bad habits, more literary.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The gradual loss of people or strength over time, especially employees who leave and are not replaced.
entries.usage: Common in HR, business and military language: *high attrition*, *attrition rates*, *through attrition* (not filling jobs when people leave, instead of firing them). In schools and studies it means students or participants dropping out. *A war of attrition* is a long fight in which each side tries to wear the other down.
entries.pattern: high / low attrition; the attrition rate; through (natural) attrition; a war of attrition
examples: The company plans to cut two hundred jobs through **attrition**, simply not replacing people who retire.
Nursing schools have high **attrition**, with many students dropping out in the first year.
The trial lost a third of its participants to **attrition** before the final follow-up.

drill.sentence: The strike became a war of {{attrition}}, with each side hoping the other would run out of money first.
drill.hint: gradually wearing the other side down (not *nerves* or *words*)

entries.related: *turnover* — the rate at which staff leave and are replaced; *churn* — business word for customers or staff leaving; *retention* — the opposite, keeping people.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Directly and clearly, with no doubt about where something belongs or what it is aimed at.
entries.usage: Common in news and analytical writing with verbs of placing and aiming: *put the blame squarely on*, *fall squarely within*, *aimed squarely at*. It adds emphasis and leaves no room for doubt. It is also used literally: *hit the ball squarely*.
entries.pattern: blame squarely on someone; squarely within / at / on; face something squarely
examples: The report puts the blame **squarely** on the airline, not the weather.
The new phone is aimed **squarely** at teenagers who want a cheaper device.
Walking the dog falls **squarely** on my son, since he's the one who begged for a puppy.

drill.sentence: The coach placed the responsibility for the loss {{squarely}} on his own shoulders.
drill.hint: right where it belonged, leaving no doubt (not *firmly*, *solely* or *entirely*)

entries.related: *directly* — more general; *firmly* — strongly, also used with *on*; *head-on* — directly and confidently, often with *face* or *tackle*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To find a way to avoid a rule, law, restriction or obstacle, often cleverly and sometimes dishonestly.
entries.usage: Common in legal, business, tech and news writing: *circumvent the rules*, *circumvent restrictions*, *circumvent a ban*. It usually suggests getting around something rather than openly breaking it. In conversation, *get around* is the natural choice.
entries.pattern: circumvent + rules / restrictions / a ban / security / the system
examples: Some landlords **circumvent** rent limits by charging extra "amenity fees."
The kids found a way to **circumvent** the parental controls on the TV within a week.
The malware **circumvents** antivirus software by disguising itself as a system update.

drill.sentence: My neighbor tried to {{circumvent}} the city's ban on backyard chickens by calling them pets.
drill.hint: find a clever way around (not *bypass*, *evade* or *dodge*)

entries.related: *get around* — the informal equivalent; *bypass* — go around something, often a system or person; *evade* — escape or avoid, often taxes or questions; *comply with* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Full of something bad or unpleasant that is common and widespread.
entries.usage: Used in journalism and serious writing, almost always after a verb: *be rife with errors*, *rife with corruption*, *rife with rumors*. Without *with*, it means widespread: *Speculation is rife*. The thing that is *rife* is almost always negative.
entries.pattern: be rife with + problems / errors / corruption / rumors; something is rife
examples: Online reviews are **rife with** fake five-star ratings, so I read the bad ones first.
The old building was **rife with** mold and had to be torn down.
The industry was **rife with** rumors of a merger, but nothing has been announced.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood used to be {{rife}} with crime, but now it's full of coffee shops and young families.
drill.hint: having lots of something bad everywhere (not *filled*, *riddled* or *overrun*)

entries.related: *riddled with* — full of holes, errors or problems; *plagued by* — repeatedly troubled by; *rampant* — spreading without control, used without *with*.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A complaint, or a lasting feeling of resentment, about being treated unfairly.
entries.usage: Common in workplace, legal and political language: *file a grievance* (a formal complaint, often through a union), *air grievances*, *a long list of grievances*. It can be a formal complaint or a private sense of injustice (*nurse a grievance*). It has two syllables: GREE-vunss.
entries.pattern: file / lodge a grievance; air grievances; a grievance against someone; nurse a grievance
examples: The union filed a formal **grievance** after two nurses were fired without warning.
At Thanksgiving, my aunt likes to air old family **grievances** over dessert.
Most of the protesters' **grievances** were about rising rent and low wages.

drill.sentence: The tenants met with the landlord to discuss their {{grievances}}, from broken heaters to the constant noise.
drill.hint: things they felt were unfair to them (not *concerns*, *issues*, *problems* or *complaints*)

entries.related: *complaint* — the everyday word; *gripe* — informal, a small complaint; *resentment* — the feeling, not the complaint itself.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Deliberately exaggerated, saying much more than is literally true, often for effect.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, reviews and discussion of how people speak: *hyperbolic language*, *hyperbolic headlines*, *a hyperbolic claim*. It is often critical, suggesting that someone is overstating things. In math, *hyperbolic* refers to a hyperbola (*hyperbolic functions*), a separate sense.
entries.pattern: hyperbolic language / headlines / claims / praise
examples: Calling it the worst day in history is a bit **hyperbolic**; we just missed the bus.
Movie trailers are full of **hyperbolic** praise like "the greatest film of the decade."
The headline was so **hyperbolic** that I assumed the article was a joke.

drill.sentence: Saying the soup nearly killed him was a little {{hyperbolic}}; it was just too salty.
drill.hint: overstated on purpose (not *dramatic*, *much* or *exaggerated*)

entries.related: *exaggerated* — plainer; *overblown* — made to seem more important than it is; *understated* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To slow down or block the movement, progress or development of something.
entries.usage: Common in formal, legal, medical and official writing: *impede progress*, *impede traffic*, *impede an investigation*. It is more formal than *hamper* or *hold up* and often refers to physical movement or official processes. The noun *impediment* means an obstacle (*a speech impediment*).
entries.pattern: impede + progress / traffic / growth / an investigation / the flow of something
examples: Parked delivery trucks constantly **impede** traffic on our narrow street.
He was charged with **impeding** a police investigation by deleting text messages.
Swelling can **impede** blood flow, so keep the injured leg raised.

drill.sentence: Fallen trees and deep mud {{impeded}} the firefighters' progress toward the burning cabin.
drill.hint: got in the way of, in formal style (not *slowed*, *hampered* or *hindered*)

entries.related: *hamper* — very close, less formal; *obstruct* — block completely, also a legal term; *facilitate* — the opposite, make easier.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lacking skill or ability, so that you do something badly or clumsily.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and conversation as a harsh criticism of people, organizations and performances: *inept management*, *an inept defense*, *socially inept*. It is much stronger and more insulting than *not very good at*. It often takes *at* (*inept at small talk*), and the noun is *ineptitude*.
entries.pattern: inept at something; socially inept; an inept attempt / handling / performance
examples: I'm completely **inept** at anything involving a sewing machine.
The city's **inept** handling of the snowstorm left some streets unplowed for a week.
He's brilliant with numbers but socially **inept**, especially at parties.

drill.sentence: The referee's {{inept}} performance in the final had fans booing him off the field.
drill.hint: lacking basic skill (not *poor* or *incompetent*)

entries.related: *incompetent* — very close, often about people at work; *clumsy* — awkward in movement or handling; *adept* — the opposite, very skilled.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A sudden, major change that causes a lot of disruption or confusion, in a person's life or in society.
entries.usage: Common in news and personal conversation: *political upheaval*, *economic upheaval*, *a period of upheaval*, *the upheaval of moving*. It is usually negative, or at least stressful. It can be countable (*a series of upheavals*) or uncountable (*years of upheaval*).
entries.pattern: a period of upheaval; political / social / emotional upheaval; cause upheaval
examples: Moving across the country with three kids was a huge **upheaval** for our family.
The 1960s were a time of great social **upheaval** in the United States.
The merger caused months of **upheaval** in the office, with people changing teams every week.

drill.sentence: After the divorce, the twins went through a lot of emotional {{upheaval}}, so we kept their routines as stable as we could.
drill.hint: sudden, major disruption (not *turmoil* or *stress*)

entries.related: *turmoil* — a state of confusion and disorder; *disruption* — interruption of normal activity; *stability* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Very strongly and sharply; it stresses how intensely someone feels or notices something.
entries.usage: Almost always with *aware* or *conscious*, or with feelings such as *embarrassed* or *uncomfortable*: *acutely aware that…*, *acutely embarrassed*. It suggests a sharp, sometimes uncomfortable sensitivity. It belongs to writing and educated speech; in casual speech *very* or *really* does the same job.
entries.pattern: acutely aware / conscious (of something / that …); acutely embarrassed / sensitive
examples: I was **acutely** aware that everyone at the table had heard my stomach growl.
After the accident, he became **acutely** sensitive to the sound of screeching brakes.
New parents are often **acutely** conscious of every cough and sneeze their baby makes.

drill.sentence: After moving to Tokyo, she was {{acutely}} aware of how loudly she talked on the train.
drill.hint: sharply and intensely (not *painfully* or *keenly*)

entries.related: *keenly* — very close, slightly more positive; *painfully* — so strongly that it hurts (*painfully aware*); *acute* — the adjective, also *severe and sudden* in medicine.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To deliberately encourage or provoke people to do something violent, illegal or harmful.
entries.usage: Common in legal language and news: *incite violence*, *incite hatred*, *incite a riot*, *incite someone to* + verb. It makes the speaker responsible for what others then do, which is why it appears in criminal charges. It sounds exactly like *insight*, so watch the spelling.
entries.pattern: incite + violence / hatred / a riot / panic; incite someone to do something
examples: Two men were arrested for **inciting** violence outside the stadium after the game.
The singer was accused of **inciting** the crowd to rush the stage, and twelve fans were hurt.
Police say the online post **incited** a riot that left three stores looted.

drill.sentence: One drunk guest tried to {{incite}} a fight between the two families at the wedding.
drill.hint: deliberately stir up (not *start*, *provoke* or *instigate*)

entries.related: *provoke* — cause a reaction, often anger; *instigate* — start something, often bad; *stir up* — informal, cause trouble or strong feelings.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Growing or developing quickly.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and business writing, mostly before nouns: *a burgeoning industry*, *a burgeoning population*, *a burgeoning romance*. It sounds positive and energetic, though it can also describe growing problems. In speech, *booming* or *fast-growing* is more usual.
entries.pattern: a burgeoning industry / market / scene / population / career
examples: Austin has a **burgeoning** food truck scene, with new trucks opening every month.
Their **burgeoning** friendship started over a shared love of terrible horror movies.
The **burgeoning** demand for GPUs has pushed prices to record highs.

drill.sentence: My niece has a {{burgeoning}} career as a children's book illustrator; her third book comes out in May.
drill.hint: quickly developing (not *growing*, *budding*, *blossoming* or *booming*)

entries.related: *booming* — growing fast, often in business; *budding* — just beginning to develop (*a budding artist*); *flourishing* — doing very well; *dwindling* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a way that is very suitable or fitting for the situation.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, travel writing and conversation, mostly in *aptly named* (often with humor) and *as someone aptly put it*. It says that a name or description fits very well, sometimes in a funny or ironic way. The adjective is *apt*.
entries.pattern: aptly named; as X aptly put it; aptly described as …
examples: Our dog, **aptly** named Chaos, has already eaten two remote controls and a shoe.
The report **aptly** describes the housing market as a game of musical chairs.
The ice cream festival took place, quite **aptly**, on the hottest day of the year.

drill.sentence: As my grandmother so {{aptly}} put it, a wedding is just a very expensive dinner party.
drill.hint: fittingly, in a way that captures it well (not *wisely* or *perfectly*)

entries.related: *fittingly* — very close; *appropriately* — suitably, more neutral; *ironically* — in a way opposite to what you'd expect.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not justified or necessary in the situation; going further than the facts call for.
entries.usage: Common in official statements, legal writing and serious conversation: *unwarranted criticism*, *unwarranted attention*, *unwarranted intrusion*. It often protests that a reaction is excessive or unfair. In analytical writing it also means *not supported by the evidence*: *an unwarranted assumption*.
entries.pattern: unwarranted criticism / attention / intrusion / fears; an unwarranted assumption
examples: The yellow card seemed completely **unwarranted**; he barely touched the other player.
That comment about your cooking was **unwarranted**, and I'm sorry.
Predicting decades of growth from three years of numbers is an **unwarranted** leap.

drill.sentence: The neighbors gave our kids a lot of {{unwarranted}} grief for shooting hoops in the driveway at four in the afternoon.
drill.hint: more than the situation called for (not *unnecessary*, *unfair*, *unjustified* or *uncalled-for*)

entries.related: *uncalled-for* — informal, about rude remarks; *unjustified* — very close; *unfounded* — not based on facts; *warranted* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Annoyed and dissatisfied, especially because you feel you have been treated badly or unfairly.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, especially about employees, customers and fans: *a disgruntled employee*, *disgruntled customers*. *A disgruntled former employee* is a stock news phrase for someone blamed for sabotage or leaks. It describes lasting resentment rather than sudden anger.
entries.pattern: a disgruntled employee / customer / fan / passenger
examples: A **disgruntled** customer left a one-star review complaining about the music.
Police believe a **disgruntled** former employee leaked the documents.
My dad was pretty **disgruntled** after the airline gave him a middle seat for a twelve-hour flight.

drill.sentence: After waiting two hours for their food, the {{disgruntled}} diners started leaving without paying.
drill.hint: fed up and dissatisfied (not *annoyed*, *angry* or *dissatisfied*)

entries.related: *dissatisfied* — more neutral; *resentful* — feeling bitter about unfair treatment; *content* — the opposite, satisfied.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Good at judging situations and people quickly, especially in a way that brings you an advantage.
entries.usage: Common in business journalism and conversation, usually as a compliment: *a shrewd businesswoman*, *a shrewd move*, *a shrewd investment*. It suggests practical cleverness and a little calculation, not academic intelligence. *A shrewd guess* is a guess that is likely to be right.
entries.pattern: a shrewd businessperson / negotiator / move / investment / guess
examples: Buying the house before the neighborhood got popular was a **shrewd** investment.
My grandmother was a **shrewd** negotiator; no car salesman ever got the better of her.
The coach made a **shrewd** substitution in the final minutes that won the game.

drill.sentence: My little brother is {{shrewd}}: he always asks Grandpa for money right after his team wins.
drill.hint: good at judging the right moment to his advantage (not *smart*, *sly* or *savvy*)

entries.related: *astute* — very close, more formal and always positive; *cunning* — clever in a dishonest way; *naive* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To put something valuable, such as a chance, a relationship or someone's safety, at risk of being lost or harmed.
entries.usage: Common in news, at work and in personal conversation: *jeopardize your career*, *jeopardize the deal*, *jeopardize someone's safety*. The object is usually something you could lose, such as a chance, a job or a friendship. The first syllable is JEP, as in the TV show *Jeopardy!*; the British spelling is *jeopardise*.
entries.pattern: jeopardize + a chance / career / relationship / safety / the deal
examples: One angry email could **jeopardize** a friendship you've had for twenty years.
He **jeopardized** his spot on the team by skipping practice three weeks in a row.
Inspectors say cuts to maintenance have **jeopardized** passenger safety on the old trains.

drill.sentence: Driving after even one drink can {{jeopardize}} your license, your job and other people's lives.
drill.hint: put in danger of being lost (not *risk*, *endanger* or *threaten*)

entries.related: *endanger* — put in danger, often lives or species; *risk* — take the chance of losing; *undermine* — weaken gradually; *safeguard* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To get a response, reaction or piece of information from someone, often by asking or doing something.
entries.usage: Common in teaching, medicine, research and journalism: *elicit a response*, *elicit information from*, *elicit laughter*, *elicit sympathy*. The reaction is the object, and the person comes after *from*. It sounds the same as *illicit* (illegal), so check the spelling.
entries.pattern: elicit + a response / reaction / laughter / information (from someone)
examples: Her emotional speech **elicited** sympathy even from her harshest critics.
The surprise quiz **elicited** a loud groan from the whole class.
The survey was designed to **elicit** honest answers about how much people really exercise.

drill.sentence: My question about her ex {{elicited}} a long silence and then a very short answer.
drill.hint: brought out as a response (not *drew*, *prompted* or *evoked*)

entries.related: *evoke* — bring a feeling or memory to mind; *prompt* — cause someone to act or speak; *illicit* — illegal, a different word.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To weaken an argument, position or effort, making it less effective or believable.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, analysis and argument: *undercut an argument*, *undercut someone's authority*, *undercut efforts to…*. It often describes actions that work against your own goals (*his behavior undercut his message*). In business it also means to sell more cheaply than a competitor; the past form is also *undercut*.
entries.pattern: undercut + an argument / message / authority / efforts / credibility
examples: Showing up late to his own talk on time management kind of **undercut** his message.
When you give in to the kids after I've said no, you **undercut** my authority.
The leaked emails seriously **undercut** the company's claim that it knew nothing.

drill.sentence: The actor's video about saving water was {{undercut}} by photos of his lawn sprinklers running at noon.
drill.hint: made less believable (not *undermined*, *weakened* or *contradicted*)

entries.related: *undermine* — very close, often gradual or secret; *weaken* — more general; *contradict* — say or show the opposite; *bolster* — the opposite, strengthen.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make a doubt, fear, belief or myth go away, usually by showing that it is wrong.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, health writing and speeches: *dispel a myth*, *dispel fears*, *dispel rumors*, *dispel the notion that…*. It often comes after *help to* or *in an attempt to*. The past tense is *dispelled*, with a double *l* in both American and British spelling.
entries.pattern: dispel + a myth / rumors / fears / doubts / the notion that …
examples: The new bakery hopes to **dispel** the myth that gluten-free bread has to taste like cardboard.
Her calm voice on the phone **dispelled** my fear that something terrible had happened.
A clear statement from the team quickly **dispelled** rumors that its star player was being traded.

drill.sentence: Five minutes with our gentle old Labrador was enough to {{dispel}} my nephew's fear of dogs.
drill.hint: make go away completely (not *cure* or *ease*)

entries.related: *debunk* — show that a claim is false, used for myths and theories; *allay* — reduce fears or doubts, formal; *fuel* — the opposite, make stronger.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Clever at quickly understanding people and situations, and good at seeing what is important.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, reviews and polite praise: *an astute observer*, *an astute observation*, *politically astute*, *astute readers will notice…*. It is more formal than *sharp* and almost always positive, unlike *shrewd*, which can suggest calculation. It describes comments and judgments as well as people.
entries.pattern: an astute observer / observation / judge of character; politically astute
examples: That's an **astute** observation; I hadn't noticed that every villain in the show is left-handed.
My aunt is an **astute** judge of character and disliked my ex-boyfriend from the start.
**Astute** readers will notice that the first chapter hints at the ending.

drill.sentence: As an {{astute}} observer of people, my aunt could tell who was dating whom long before anyone announced it.
drill.hint: sharp at reading people and situations (not *attentive* or *avid*)

entries.related: *shrewd* — similar, but suggests using cleverness for your own advantage; *perceptive* — quick to notice and understand; *obtuse* — the opposite, slow to understand.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Bold and shameless; done openly, without any attempt to hide it and without embarrassment.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about crimes, lies and bad behavior: *a brazen theft*, *a brazen lie*, *a brazen attack in broad daylight*. It is critical but often carries disbelief at the nerve involved. *Brazen it out* means to act confidently as if you had done nothing wrong.
entries.pattern: a brazen lie / theft / attack / attempt; brazen it out
examples: In a **brazen** daylight robbery, thieves drove a truck through the front window of a jewelry store.
My brother told a **brazen** lie about eating the last slice, with chocolate still on his face.
The **brazen** price hike angered fans, who were suddenly paying twice as much for the same seats.

drill.sentence: Someone stole a package right off our porch in the middle of the afternoon, which was pretty {{brazen}}.
drill.hint: done openly, without any shame (not *bold*, *gutsy*, *ballsy* or *shameless*)

entries.related: *shameless* — very close; *audacious* — bold and willing to take risks, can be positive; *blatant* — very obvious; *sheepish* — the opposite, embarrassed.

entries.label: adjective (before a noun)
entries.meaning: New and still developing, so not yet strong, experienced or established.
entries.usage: Common in news and business writing, almost always before a noun: *a fledgling company*, *a fledgling democracy*, *a fledgling career*. It suggests fragility as well as promise. Literally, a *fledgling* is a young bird that is just learning to fly.
entries.pattern: a fledgling company / business / industry / career / democracy
examples: A single bad review can sink a **fledgling** restaurant in its first few months.
My cousin left a stable job to focus on her **fledgling** jewelry business.
The country's **fledgling** democracy held its first free election in 1994.

drill.sentence: The town's {{fledgling}} soccer league has only six teams so far, but it's growing every season.
drill.hint: new and still finding its feet (not *new*, *young* or *budding*)

entries.related: *budding* — beginning to develop, often about people (*a budding artist*); *nascent* — formal, just starting to exist; *established* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A statement or argument that tries to show that a claim or accusation is false.
entries.usage: Common in law, debate, peer review and journalism: *a rebuttal to* or *of* something, *in rebuttal*, *issue a rebuttal*. It suggests a formal, reasoned answer rather than a quick reply. The verb is *rebut*; in casual speech people say *respond to* or *push back on*.
entries.pattern: a rebuttal to / of something; in rebuttal; write / issue a rebuttal
examples: The newspaper published her **rebuttal** to the critic's review the following week.
The company issued a detailed **rebuttal**, denying every claim in the lawsuit.
In the debate, each side gets two minutes for a **rebuttal** after the opening speeches.

drill.sentence: My brother answered Mom's list of reasons why he couldn't get a dog with a three-page {{rebuttal}}.
drill.hint: formal counter-case (not *response*, *reply* or *counterargument*)

entries.related: *refutation* — proof that a claim is wrong, more formal; *retort* — a quick, sharp reply; *response* — neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Weak and unconvincing, so that it does not stand up to questioning.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, journalism and law about reasons and proof: *a flimsy excuse*, *flimsy evidence*, *a flimsy argument*, *on flimsy grounds*. It is critical and suggests that something could easily be knocked down, like a thin structure. The literal sense is about thin, light, weak objects (*a flimsy plastic chair*).
entries.pattern: a flimsy excuse / argument / pretext; flimsy evidence; on flimsy grounds
examples: He canceled dinner with some **flimsy** excuse about having to wash his car.
The case against her was based on **flimsy** evidence and was quickly thrown out.
Firing him on such **flimsy** grounds could easily lead to a lawsuit.

drill.sentence: "The dog ate my homework" is about the {{flimsiest}} excuse a kid can come up with.
drill.hint: least convincing (not *lamest*, *weakest*, *feeblest* or *oldest*)

entries.related: *lame* — informal, for excuses; *tenuous* — very weak, often about a link or connection; *compelling* — the opposite, convincing.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A division or contrast between two things that are presented as completely opposite or separate.
entries.usage: Common in academic writing, journalism and serious discussion: *a dichotomy between A and B*, *a false dichotomy*. *False dichotomy* criticizes an argument that offers only two options when there are more. In casual speech it can sound pretentious; *an either-or choice* is plainer.
entries.pattern: a dichotomy between A and B; a false dichotomy
examples: The old **dichotomy** between work and home has blurred now that so many people work remotely.
Saying you must choose between a career and kids is a false **dichotomy**.
The paper challenges the **dichotomy** between nature and nurture in language learning.

drill.sentence: People talk about the {{dichotomy}} between "book smart" and "street smart," but most people I know are a bit of both.
drill.hint: a sharp division into two supposed opposites (not *divide*, *distinction* or *contrast*)

entries.related: *contrast* — a difference, more neutral; *binary* — a two-part system, now common for categories; *continuum* — the opposite idea, a range without sharp divisions.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The time when someone or something was most successful, popular or powerful.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, journalism and reviews, usually about the past and with a possessive or *in its heyday*: *in his heyday*, *the heyday of the shopping mall*. It often carries nostalgia or a hint that the success is over. It is normally singular.
entries.pattern: in someone's / its heyday; the heyday of something
examples: In its **heyday**, this mall had three department stores and a skating rink.
My dad still talks about his **heyday** as a college quarterback.
The 1990s were the **heyday** of the video rental store.

drill.sentence: Grandma says that in her {{heyday}} she could dance all night and still make it to work by eight.
drill.hint: period of greatest success and energy (not *prime*, *youth* or *day*)

entries.related: *prime* — the best period of life or ability, often physical; *golden age* — a period of great achievement, often for a field or country; *decline* — what comes after.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not supported by any facts or evidence at all.
entries.usage: Common in news, legal statements and denials: *baseless claims*, *baseless accusations*, *baseless rumors*, *completely baseless*. It is a strong, combative word, often used to dismiss an accusation outright. It is stronger than *unfounded*, which is also the usual word for worries that turn out to be unnecessary.
entries.pattern: baseless claims / accusations / rumors / allegations; completely / entirely baseless
examples: The judge dismissed the lawsuit, calling the claims against the hospital **baseless**.
A neighbor spread **baseless** rumors that we were selling the house, and now realtors keep calling.
The viral post made the **baseless** claim that drinking hot water kills viruses in your throat.

drill.sentence: He accused his roommate of stealing his headphones, but the accusation was {{baseless}}: they were in his own backpack.
drill.hint: without any evidence at all (not *unfounded*, *false* or *bogus*)

entries.related: *unfounded* — similar, softer, also for fears; *groundless* — very close; *spurious* — false and misleading, often about arguments or links; *well-founded* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To disrupt a plan, process or conversation so that it cannot continue as intended.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and conversation: *derail talks*, *derail a project*, *derail someone's career*, *derail the conversation*. It suggests a sudden event or action that throws things off course. Literally, a train *derails* or *is derailed* when it leaves the tracks.
entries.pattern: derail + talks / plans / a career / a conversation / a project
examples: A knee injury **derailed** her plans to run the Boston Marathon.
The negotiations were nearly **derailed** by a dispute over who would pay for parking.
Every team meeting gets **derailed** when someone brings up the office temperature.

drill.sentence: The argument about whose turn it was to do the dishes completely {{derailed}} our movie night.
drill.hint: threw off course (not *ruined*, *wrecked* or *destroyed*)

entries.related: *sidetrack* — distract from the main subject, milder; *disrupt* — interrupt, more general; *torpedo* — destroy a plan on purpose, informal.
